behavior.overview: This repository provides a modular, Java-based e-commerce application implementation utilizing Domain-Driven Design (DDD) principles. It manages the end-to-end flow of retail operations including product cataloging, shopping cart management, order placement, warehouse inventory, payment processing, and delivery dispatching.

partitions.name: Portal
partitions.functionality: Acts as the user-facing entry point by handling web requests and orchestrating business workflows such as placing an order from a cart.

partitions.name: Sales
partitions.functionality: Manages core sales entities including product catalog listings, customer shopping carts, and order life-cycle tracking.

partitions.name: Warehouse
partitions.functionality: Handles stock management, tracking available goods, and responding to domain events triggered by order placement or delivery status changes.

partitions.name: Billing
partitions.functionality: Processes payments for orders, including record keeping and status updates triggered by domain events.

partitions.name: Shipping
partitions.functionality: Manages delivery preparations and coordinates the dispatching saga to track and update the status of shipments.

blueprint.selected_pattern: Strangler Fig migration from a Java modular monolith to a selectively decomposed, event-driven architecture (one extracted service, monolith retained)
blueprint.rationale: The repository is already a well-bounded DDD modular monolith (Portal, Sales, Warehouse, Billing, Shipping) with in-process domain events and a single SQL schema, and the ArchUnit module tests (CleanModulesArchTest.java, CleanCodeArchTest.java) show the module seams are actively enforced. The stated drivers are the non-functional requirements 'Support higher and uneven traffic', 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' and 'Reliable core purchasing flows', plus maintainability, under an explicit cost-conscious, incremental, no-mandatory-cloud constraint. A full microservices decomposition would multiply operational cost without evidence of per-module scaling, ownership or compliance drivers. The smallest decomposition that satisfies the requirements is therefore: keep the monolith as the transactional core, extract only the read-heavy Catalog & Pricing capability (whose load profile is driven by browsing traffic and is independent of back-office fulfilment work), put an edge routing gateway in front for coexistence and independent scaling, and make cross-boundary domain events durable so the purchase flow stays consistent under partial failure. The pattern label names the transition because the target state is deliberately a monolith plus a small number of extracted services, reached incrementally.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Retail Customer actors browse the catalog, build a cart, place an order, pay, and follow delivery status. Warehouse Staff actors maintain stock, prepare and dispatch shipments, and review stuck orders or payments. Business stability is the primary constraint: nothing in this design requires a big-bang cut-over, and every step is releasable and reversible on its own. The change customers feel is that promotion-driven browsing spikes no longer degrade checkout, because catalog browsing runs on its own independently scalable service and back-office fulfilment work no longer competes with customer-facing requests â€” this is how the design meets 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions'. The change the business feels addresses 'Reliable core purchasing flows': the purchase chain (cart to order to payment to stock to shipment) survives a failing step because work is retried, duplicates are ignored, and anything that cannot complete becomes visible to staff instead of silently disappearing. The change the delivery team feels is that catalog/pricing can be changed and deployed on its own cadence, while Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module keep the low-friction single-deployment model they have today. Costs stay bounded: the existing Java/Spring stack and existing relational database technology are retained, and the only genuinely new infrastructure is a message broker, an edge gateway and an observability stack, each justified by a stated requirement.
blueprint.technical_view:
Target state. Two deployables plus supporting infrastructure, consumed by two explicitly external actors (Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff) and integrating one external system (External Payment Provider). (1) Commerce Core Application â€” the existing Spring Boot Java monolith, retaining the Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module, Shipping Delivery Module and Storefront Portal, backed by the Core Commerce SQL Database. (2) Catalog & Pricing Service â€” a separately deployable Spring Boot Java service owning product, category and price data in the Catalog & Pricing Database. In front of both sits the Edge Routing Gateway, which routes customer-facing catalog and product-detail traffic to the Catalog & Pricing Service and everything else to the Storefront Portal, allowing the two deployables to be scaled with different replica counts and enabling gradual traffic shifting during extraction. This routing seam is the direct technical answer to the non-functional requirements 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions'.

Communication. Within the Commerce Core Application, modules keep their current in-process, interface-based collaboration and their existing DDD domain events (OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, DeliveryPrepared, DeliveryDispatched, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed) â€” this preserves the transactional consistency of the purchase chain in one database and avoids distributed transactions where no driver demands them. Cross-boundary communication (Commerce Core Application to/from Catalog & Pricing Service) is asynchronous over the Domain Event Backbone for state propagation (price and publication changes, out-of-stock signals) and synchronous HTTP only where a request must be answered inline (price/availability validation when an item is added to the cart, priced-line-item snapshot at checkout). Every event published across a boundary is written through a transactional outbox in the publisher's own database and relayed to the broker, so publication is atomic with the state change that caused it.

Reliability â€” this is the design's explicit answer to the non-functional requirement 'Reliable core purchasing flows'. Each state-changing purchase operation carries an idempotency key (cart-id/checkout-token for order placement, payment reference for payment confirmation, order-id for dispatch), so retries and duplicate deliveries converge to one effect. The existing DispatchingSaga is generalised into the choreographed compensation model for the order lifecycle: stock reservation failure rejects the order and releases the reservation, payment failure leaves the order unpaid and retryable, and exhausted retries land in a dead-letter view surfaced to staff. Failure-injection tests per core step validate that order, payment, stock and shipment data stay consistent.

Data. No store migration. The Core Commerce SQL Database remains the existing relational schema; catalog, category and price tables move to the Catalog & Pricing Database as part of extraction, with the Commerce Core Application keeping only the product identifiers and priced snapshots it already persists in orders and cart items. Cross-boundary reads are by identifier plus cached projection, never by shared table access; schema-level separation is introduced before the physical split so the split is a deployment event rather than a rewrite.

Observability. The Observability & Alerting Stack collects metrics, logs and distributed traces from the Edge Routing Gateway, the Storefront Portal, the Catalog & Pricing Service, all domain modules and the Domain Event Backbone, exposes response time and error rate per flow (browse, cart, checkout, payment) and counts of stuck orders, payments and shipments, and raises alerts on agreed thresholds to Warehouse Staff and operators. Thresholds and peak-load multiples are to be agreed and measured; no numeric target is asserted here.

constraints_addressed: Cloud: no provider mandated; all components are deployable on the existing runtime (JVM/Spring Boot, container or VM) and are provider-neutral. Managed equivalents may be substituted without design change.

Budget: exactly one service is extracted; the remaining four domain modules stay in the existing deployable. New infrastructure is limited to a message broker, a gateway and an observability stack, each tied to a stated requirement.

Non-functional 'Support higher and uneven traffic': read-heavy catalog/pricing traffic is separated behind the Edge Routing Gateway and scales independently of back-office fulfilment (FEAT-008). No numeric peak target is asserted; the peak-load multiple must be agreed and measured.

Non-functional 'Responsive customer-facing interactions': browse and product-detail load is removed from the transactional deployable, per-flow response time is measured by the Observability & Alerting Stack, and the responsiveness target is to be agreed with the business rather than asserted here.

Non-functional 'Reliable core purchasing flows': the purchase chain keeps single-database transactional consistency in the Core Commerce SQL Database, cross-boundary events are published through a transactional outbox, all state-changing operations are idempotent, compensation is choreographed via the dispatching saga, and exhausted retries surface in a dead-letter view (FEAT-009).
Compliance: no compliance requirements were stated. Payment card data is not stored; only provider references are persisted, keeping cardholder-data scope out of the system.
Migration: strangler-fig sequence with schema separation before physical split, dual-routing during extraction, and no step requiring simultaneous cut-over of all modules (FEAT-010).
assumptions: Assumption: the application is Spring Boot based (Maven wrapper, Thymeleaf templates, JDBC repositories in the repository), and Spring's in-process ApplicationEventPublisher backs the current EventPublisher abstraction.

Assumption: peak traffic is dominated by anonymous catalog browsing and product-detail reads rather than by checkout write volume; this is the premise for extracting Catalog & Pricing first and must be confirmed with production traffic data.

Assumption: the current deployment is a single instance or a small horizontally scaled set of the monolith behind an existing entry point; the Edge Routing Gateway replaces or fronts that entry point.

Assumption: customer identity/session handling exists sufficiently for cart persistence across sessions (repository shows cart identification via cookies); identified-customer cart persistence (FEAT-003) may require an identity capability not present in the repository.
Assumption: the exact responsiveness, availability and error-rate targets are not yet defined; acceptance criteria are stated qualitatively until the business agrees numbers.
Assumption: Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff are human actors external to the system boundary; they are modelled as external participants and are not built or deployed by this design.
open_risks: Risk: extracting Catalog & Pricing introduces a synchronous dependency from Sales Cart Module at add-to-cart time; if the Catalog & Pricing Service is unavailable, add-to-cart fails. Mitigation (to be designed): short-lived price/publication cache in the Commerce Core Application with an explicit staleness bound.

Risk: price consistency between display and checkout across a service boundary (FEAT-002) depends on the priced snapshot being taken at cart-add and re-validated at checkout; a race remains between price change and checkout and must be resolved by an agreed business rule.
Risk: the repository shows no existing message broker; introducing the Domain Event Backbone adds an operational component the team may not yet run, plus outbox relay and dead-letter handling.
Risk: FEAT-003's cross-session cart persistence for identified customers has no visible identity/authentication capability in the repository; scope may be larger than this design assumes.

Risk: FEAT-001 catalog authoring (create/update/deactivate/publish) is only partially evidenced in the repository (read-side finders dominate); the write side of catalog management may need to be built rather than extracted.

Risk: without agreed numeric SLOs, the peak-load and failure-injection acceptance criteria in FEAT-008 and FEAT-009 cannot yet be validated objectively, so the 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirement can currently only be validated qualitatively.

migration_steps.title: Harden module seams and establish baseline observability
migration_steps.objective: Make the current modular monolith measurable and its boundaries explicit before anything moves, so later steps are low-risk and their effect is visible. First because every subsequent step depends on knowing the real traffic profile and on enforced boundaries.
changes: Extend the existing ArchUnit module tests so every cross-module call goes through a published module interface only.

Deploy the Observability & Alerting Stack and instrument Storefront Portal, Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module with metrics, logs and distributed tracing.
Measure the real traffic split between catalog browsing and transactional flows to confirm the extraction premise.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: No structural or data change; the Commerce Core Application remains the single deployable against the Core Commerce SQL Database.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Per-flow response time and error rate are visible for browse, cart, checkout and payment, and boundary tests fail on any direct cross-module internal access.

migration_steps.title: Separate catalog and pricing schema ownership inside the Core Commerce SQL Database
migration_steps.objective: Turn the future service boundary into a data boundary while still inside one deployable, so the later physical split is a deployment event rather than a rewrite. Second because data coupling, not code coupling, is the expensive part of extraction.
changes: Move product, category and price tables into a dedicated schema within the Core Commerce SQL Database owned solely by the catalog and pricing code.
Replace any join-based cross-module access to those tables from Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module and Warehouse Inventory Module with calls to the catalog module interface.
Confirm that Sales Order Module persists a priced line-item snapshot so orders never depend on live price lookups.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Single database instance, two logically owned schemas; all access remains transactional and in-process, so no consistency change occurs yet.
migration_steps.exit_condition: No SQL statement outside the catalog and pricing code references catalog, category or price tables.

migration_steps.title: Introduce the Domain Event Backbone with a transactional outbox
migration_steps.objective: Provide durable, retryable, idempotent cross-boundary messaging before any boundary becomes a network boundary, directly serving the 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirement. Third because the extracted service and the reliability requirement (FEAT-009) both depend on it.
changes: Deploy the Domain Event Backbone (message broker) and add an outbox table plus relay to the Core Commerce SQL Database.

Route the existing OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed, DeliveryPrepared and DeliveryDispatched domain events through the outbox, keeping delivery semantics compatible with today's listeners.

migration_steps.exit_condition: A documented failure-injection test on payment, stock and shipping steps leaves order, payment, stock and shipment data consistent, and exhausted retries appear in the dead-letter view.

migration_steps.objective: Create the routing seam that later allows traffic to be shifted to an extracted service and allows differential scaling, with no behavioural change. Fourth because it must be proven neutral before it carries a split.
changes: Deploy the Edge Routing Gateway as the single entry point for Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff traffic.
Route all traffic to the Storefront Portal of the Commerce Core Application initially.
Emit gateway request metrics and traces to the Observability & Alerting Stack.

migration_steps.exit_condition: All Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff traffic flows through the Edge Routing Gateway with unchanged functional behaviour and no measurable regression against the step-1 baseline.

migration_steps.title: Extract the Catalog & Pricing Service and its Catalog & Pricing Database
migration_steps.objective: Deliver the actual scaling benefit by making the read-heavy browsing capability independently deployable and scalable. Fifth because it is only safe once seams, data ownership, messaging and routing exist.

Promote the separated catalog schema into the standalone Catalog & Pricing Database.

Subscribe the Catalog & Pricing Service to out-of-stock events from Warehouse Inventory Module via the Domain Event Backbone.

migration_steps.exit_condition: All catalog browse and product-detail traffic is served by the Catalog & Pricing Service, the Commerce Core Application no longer reads catalog tables, and full regression tests for all core purchasing flows pass.

migration_steps.title: Tune independent scaling and validate the target state
migration_steps.objective: Confirm the modernization actually satisfies the 'Support higher and uneven traffic', 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' and 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirements, and formally record what remains in the monolith. migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Steady target state: two deployables, two databases, one event backbone; further extraction is explicitly deferred, not implied.
migration_steps.exit_condition: The agreed peak-load and failure-injection tests pass within the thresholds the business has by then defined, and alerts fire correctly when those thresholds are breached.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Modernize via a Strangler Fig migration that retains the modular monolith as the transactional core
adrs.context: The system is a Java modular monolith with enforced DDD module boundaries (CleanModulesArchTest.java) and a single SQL schema. The business wants better scalability, maintainability and evolvability, but explicitly asks for cost-conscious incremental change, no unnecessary operational complexity and no large platform migration, while preserving business stability.
adrs.decision: Adopt a Strangler Fig migration: keep the existing monolith as the Commerce Core Application holding the transactional purchase chain, and extract capabilities into standalone services only where a concrete driver exists. Every step is independently releasable and reversible; no big-bang cut-over is planned.
adrs.rationale: The retrieved literature attributes microservice benefits mainly to independent scaling of services with distinct load profiles. Only the catalog/browse capability in this system has such a distinct profile; Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module share one transactional purchase flow, one team, one release cadence and one consistency boundary, so splitting them would add distributed-transaction and operational cost without a matching driver and would work against the 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirement. Incremental extraction also directly satisfies the stability and budget constraints.
alternatives_considered: Full decomposition into per-module microservices (Portal, Sales, Warehouse, Billing, Shipping) â€” rejected: no scaling, ownership, compliance or availability driver per module, and it would fragment the order/payment/stock consistency boundary.
Leave the monolith unchanged and scale it vertically/horizontally as a whole â€” rejected: browsing spikes would continue to consume capacity needed by checkout and back-office fulfilment (FEAT-008).
Rewrite on a new platform â€” rejected by the explicit no-large-migration budget constraint.
positive_consequences: Operational footprint grows by one service rather than five.
The purchase chain keeps single-database transactional consistency.
Each modernization step can be rolled back independently (FEAT-010).
negative_consequences: Scaling granularity remains coarse for the transactional core.
Future extraction of a second service will require repeating the seam and data-ownership work.

adrs.title: ADR-002: Extract Catalog and Pricing as the first and only standalone service
adrs.context: Traffic is described as higher and uneven, driven by customer-facing browsing during promotions, while warehouse and fulfilment workloads stay comparatively flat. Catalog and pricing data is read-dominant, largely immutable between edits, and cacheable; the repository's catalog package is overwhelmingly composed of read-side finders (FindProducts, FindCategories, FindProductsFromCategory).
adrs.decision: Extract catalog, category and pricing into a single standalone Catalog & Pricing Service with its own Catalog & Pricing Database. Pricing is kept inside the same service as catalog rather than split out separately.
adrs.rationale: Catalog/browse meets several separation drivers at once: a materially different load profile from the transactional core, independent scaling characteristics, a clearly separate data ownership boundary, and fault isolation for the customer-facing read path â€” which together serve 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions'. Pricing, by contrast, meets none of them independently â€” a price is an attribute of a sellable product, changes through the same authoring workflow, and shares the same read path and consistency needs, so a separate pricing service would create a chatty network hop and a split transaction for no benefit. Grouping them is the smallest decomposition that satisfies FEAT-008.
alternatives_considered: Separate Catalog Service and Pricing Service â€” rejected: no independent scaling, ownership or consistency driver; would split one aggregate across a network boundary.

Extract the Storefront Portal (web layer) instead â€” rejected: the Portal is an orchestration layer tightly coupled to Sales, Billing and Shipping module interfaces; extracting it would create synchronous chatter without isolating the read-heavy load.

Add a read replica or cache in front of the monolith only â€” rejected as insufficient: it does not decouple deployment or protect checkout capacity from browse-driven resource consumption, though caching is retained inside the extracted service.
positive_consequences: Browse traffic scales independently of fulfilment and checkout capacity.
Catalog and pricing can be released on their own cadence.
Failure of the catalog read path does not take down order or payment processing.
negative_consequences: Add-to-cart gains a synchronous cross-service dependency for price and publication validation.
Price display and checkout pricing now span a boundary and require snapshot plus re-validation rules.
One additional deployable and database to operate.

adrs.title: ADR-003: Introduce a durable domain event backbone with the transactional outbox pattern
adrs.context: The purchase chain is already event-choreographed in-process (OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed, DeliveryPrepared, DeliveryDispatched, plus a DispatchingSaga). In-process publication is lost on process failure and cannot cross the new service boundary, yet the non-functional requirement 'Reliable core purchasing flows' and FEAT-009 require that a payment outcome is never lost and that failures are retried and made visible.
adrs.decision: Introduce a message broker as the Domain Event Backbone, publish all cross-boundary and reliability-critical domain events through a transactional outbox written in the same database transaction as the state change, and relay them asynchronously with retries and a dead-letter view.
adrs.rationale: The outbox makes event publication atomic with the state change that caused it, which is the only way to guarantee that a committed payment or stock reservation always produces its downstream event. Asynchronous events also preserve the existing decoupled choreography while allowing the Catalog & Pricing Service to receive availability updates without a synchronous callback. The retrieved event-driven migration work supports asynchronous domain events as the natural fit for e-commerce processes.
alternatives_considered: Keep in-process Spring events only â€” rejected: events cannot cross the service boundary and are lost on crash between commit and publication.
Synchronous HTTP calls between all steps â€” rejected: couples availability of payment, stock and shipping to each other and worsens behaviour under spike load.
Dual-write to the broker without an outbox â€” rejected: creates a window where state is committed but the event is never published.
positive_consequences: No committed business state change loses its downstream event.
Retries and dead-lettering give Warehouse Staff visibility of stuck orders, payments and shipments.
The existing choreography and saga survive the service split largely unchanged.
negative_consequences: A broker becomes new operational infrastructure the team must run and monitor.
At-least-once delivery forces idempotent consumers everywhere (see ADR-006).
Eventual consistency becomes observable in some cross-boundary reads.

adrs.title: ADR-004: Retain Java, Spring Boot and the relational SQL store, splitting schema ownership instead of migrating data platforms
adrs.context: The detected stack is Java (6,613 LOC) with SQL schema and JDBC repositories and Thymeleaf templates. The context record asks to reuse the existing deployment and technology approach and to introduce new infrastructure only when clearly justified, on a cost-conscious budget.
adrs.decision: Implement the Catalog & Pricing Service in the same Java/Spring Boot stack and on the same relational database technology as the Commerce Core Application. Achieve data separation by moving catalog, category and price tables into a dedicated schema first and then into the standalone Catalog & Pricing Database, rather than adopting a different data store.
adrs.rationale: No stated requirement exceeds what a relational store handles well: catalog reads are key- and category-indexed lookups, pricing needs transactional correctness and history, and read scaling is achievable with the extracted service's own instances, caching and, if needed, read replicas. Changing language or data store would discard working, test-covered code and add migration risk with no requirement-linked benefit, contradicting the budget and stability constraints.
alternatives_considered: Move the catalog to a document store or dedicated search engine â€” deferred, not adopted: justified only if full-text/faceted search requirements emerge that the relational store cannot serve; no such requirement is stated.
Implement the extracted service in a different language â€” rejected: no requirement-linked justification; would fragment skills and tooling.
Introduce a shared database between the two deployables â€” rejected: would recreate the coupling the extraction is meant to remove.
positive_consequences: Existing code, tests, build tooling and operational knowledge are reused.
No data-platform migration risk and no new licensing or skill costs.
Schema-first separation makes the physical split a low-risk deployment event.
negative_consequences: Two databases of the same technology to back up, patch and monitor.
Advanced search/faceting, if later required, will need an additional decision.

adrs.title: ADR-005: Introduce an edge routing gateway as the coexistence and differential-scaling seam
adrs.context: Extraction requires that customer traffic can be moved from the monolith to the new service gradually and rolled back, and the non-functional requirements 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' (FEAT-008) require that customer-facing read capacity scale without scaling back-office processing. Today all traffic from Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff terminates in the single monolith deployable.
adrs.decision: Place an Edge Routing Gateway in front of both deployables as the single entry point for Retail Customer and Warehouse Staff, routing catalog browse and product-detail paths to the Catalog & Pricing Service and all other paths to the Storefront Portal, with the ability to shift traffic progressively and revert.
adrs.rationale: The gateway is what makes the strangler pattern operationally safe: it decouples the URL contract seen by clients from the deployable that serves it, so extraction becomes a routing change rather than a client change. It is also the natural place to apply per-route rate limiting and to measure per-flow latency and error rate for FEAT-011. It is introduced and proven pass-through before it carries any split.
alternatives_considered: Client-side or DNS-level routing â€” rejected: cannot shift traffic gradually or revert quickly, and splits the observability point.
Let the monolith proxy catalog requests to the new service â€” rejected: keeps monolith capacity on the critical path of the traffic the extraction is meant to offload.
positive_consequences: Progressive traffic shifting and instant rollback during extraction.
Independent replica counts and autoscaling per deployable.
One place to measure customer-facing latency and error rate.
negative_consequences: A new component on the critical path that must itself be highly available.
Routing rules become configuration that must be versioned and tested.

adrs.title: ADR-006: Make the purchase chain idempotent and compensating rather than distributed-transactional
adrs.context: The non-functional requirement 'Reliable core purchasing flows' and FEAT-009 require that retries never double-charge, that no downstream failure leaves an order in an undefined state, and that exhausted retries are visible. The Domain Event Backbone delivers at least once, and the External Payment Provider can time out after authorizing.
adrs.decision: Give every state-changing purchase operation an explicit idempotency key (checkout token for order placement, payment reference for payment confirmation, order identifier for stock reservation and dispatch), deduplicate on the consumer side, and extend the existing dispatching saga into the choreographed compensation model for the order lifecycle (stock shortfall rejects the order and releases the reservation; payment failure leaves the order retryable). No two-phase commit is used across the service boundary.
adrs.rationale: The order/payment/stock/shipment steps that remain in the Commerce Core Application share one database and stay transactional there; only cross-boundary interactions are eventual, and for those idempotency plus compensation is cheaper and more available than distributed transactions. This is the concrete mechanism by which 'Reliable core purchasing flows' is delivered. Idempotency is also mandatory because at-least-once delivery was accepted in ADR-003, and it is what makes the exactly-once order state transitions in FEAT-004 and FEAT-005 achievable.
alternatives_considered: Distributed transactions / two-phase commit across services â€” rejected: availability and complexity cost, and the literature flags transaction management as a core microservice challenge.
Best-effort retries without idempotency keys â€” rejected: risks duplicate orders and double charges.
Orchestrated saga with a central coordinator â€” deferred: the existing choreographed DispatchingSaga already covers the flow; a coordinator can be revisited if the flow grows.
positive_consequences: Duplicate events and client retries converge to a single business effect.
Every failure path ends in a defined order state or a visible dead-letter entry.
No availability coupling introduced by distributed locking.
negative_consequences: Idempotency keys and dedup stores must be maintained per consumer.
Compensating logic is business-specific and must be tested with failure injection.

adrs.title: ADR-007: Establish centralized metrics, tracing and alerting before any extraction
adrs.context: FEAT-011 requires per-flow response time and error rate, counts of stuck orders/payments/shipments, threshold alerts and end-to-end request tracing. The system currently spans modules in one process and will soon span two deployables and a broker, and the extraction premise (browse-dominated peaks) is unverified. Without measurement, neither 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' nor 'Reliable core purchasing flows' can be evidenced.
adrs.decision: Deploy an Observability & Alerting Stack collecting metrics, structured logs and distributed traces from the Edge Routing Gateway, the Catalog & Pricing Service, the Storefront Portal and all domain modules of the Commerce Core Application, plus queue and dead-letter metrics from the Domain Event Backbone, and surface dashboards and alerts to Warehouse Staff and operators. It is introduced in the first migration step, before any component moves.
adrs.rationale: Extraction decisions and peak-load claims cannot be validated without baseline measurement, and cross-deployable failures are not diagnosable without correlated traces. Placing it first also means every later step's effect is observable and reversible on evidence rather than opinion. Alert thresholds are deliberately left to be agreed with the business rather than asserted here.
alternatives_considered: Add observability after the extraction â€” rejected: leaves no baseline to compare against and makes the first cross-service incident undiagnosable.
Rely on application logs only â€” rejected: no correlated tracing across the boundary and no threshold alerting.
positive_consequences: Baseline evidence for the extraction premise and for peak-load validation.
Stuck orders, payments and shipments become operationally visible.
Single request traceable across gateway, monolith modules and the extracted service.
negative_consequences: Additional infrastructure and instrumentation effort before any functional benefit is delivered.
Thresholds remain undefined until the business agrees targets.

components.name: Domain Event Backbone

components.description: New infrastructure introduced in migration step 3, before any component is extracted. Publishers write to an outbox in their own database and a relay forwards to the broker, giving atomic publication. Delivery is at least once, so all consumers deduplicate on an idempotency key (ADR-006). Provides retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue whose contents are surfaced to Warehouse Staff.

Outbox-relayed events from Catalog & Pricing Database
outputs: Event deliveries to Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module, Shipping Delivery Module and Catalog & Pricing Service
Dead-letter entries for Warehouse Staff review
Queue depth, retry and dead-letter metrics to Observability & Alerting Stack
technology_choices: A single self-hostable broker sized to current volumes (e.g. RabbitMQ or Kafka), chosen to keep operational footprint minimal and to remain cloud-provider neutral
security_considerations: Authenticated, TLS-protected client connections with per-service credentials

Avoid placing personal data in event payloads beyond identifiers where possible
scalability_considerations: Buffers spikes so producers are not blocked by slow consumers
Consumer concurrency tunable per event type; dead-letter depth is an early warning signal

components.name: Observability & Alerting Stack
components.purpose: Collects metrics, logs and distributed traces and raises threshold alerts so spikes and failures are detected early, providing the evidence for 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' and 'Reliable core purchasing flows'.
components.description: New infrastructure introduced in migration step 1, before any structural change, to establish a baseline and validate the extraction premise. Threshold alerts to Warehouse Staff and operators
Baseline and peak-load evidence for migration validation

judgment_reasons.repo_grounding: The design is tied to concrete repository facts rather than being generic: it names the actual packages (com/ttulka/ecommerce/portal with CartController/CatalogController/OrderController/PlaceOrderFromCart, sales/cart CartJdbc, sales/order PlaceOrder/OrderJdbc, billing/payment CollectPayment/OrderPlacedListener, warehouse FetchGoods/InStock, shipping/dispatching DispatchingSaga), the real in-process domain events (OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed, DeliveryPrepared, DeliveryDispatched), the enforced boundary tests (CleanModulesArchTest.java, CleanCodeArchTest.java), the JDBC/Thymeleaf/schema.sql stack and the read-dominant catalog finders (FindProducts, FindCategories, FindProductsFromCategory) as the evidence for extracting Catalog & Pricing. Assumptions also flag repository-evidenced gaps (cookie-based cart identity, missing catalog write side).
judgment_reasons.flaw_detection: The design targets the stated goal (maintainability/scalability/evolvability with business stability) and the stated problem (uneven traffic on a modular monolith) via a structural cause argument: browse-driven read load competes with the transactional purchase chain in a single deployable and single schema. Decomposition quality is defended, not module-mirrored â€” only Catalog & Pricing becomes standalone, with a stated boundary rationale (distinct spike-driven load profile, independent scaling, separate data ownership, fault isolation for the read path), and ADR-002 explicitly rejects a separate Pricing service and Portal extraction; ADR-001 rejects the five-service split because Cart/Order/Payment/Inventory/Delivery share one consistency boundary and release cadence. Migration is coherent for a no-downtime objective: observability baseline â†’ schema-ownership separation inside the existing DB â†’ outbox/broker with per-event-type cutover â†’ pass-through gateway proven neutral â†’ progressive traffic shifting with monolith catalog read path as fallback and catalog tables dropped only after fallback retirement â†’ scaling validation. Each step has an exit condition and a coexistence/rollback statement, so no big-bang cutover is implied.
judgment_reasons.adr_soundness: Each ADR states context, decision, rationale, alternatives with reasons for rejection/deferral, and both positive and negative consequences (e.g. ADR-002 accepts a synchronous add-to-cart dependency and price-snapshot race; ADR-003 accepts broker operations and observable eventual consistency). judgment_reasons.best_practice_grounding: Claims are either repository-evidenced, tied to the two retrieved documents, or explicitly labelled as assumptions/risks. Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

In response to the complications of microservices deployment, particularly in cloud-based e-commerce, this study proposes a taxonomy to address these challenges. Microservices, while promising in terms of flexibility and scalability, introduce issues such as service integration, data consistency, and transaction management. Our taxonomy provides a structured approach to these challenges by clearly defining service boundaries, suggesting data management patterns, and proposing robust communication protocols between services, allowing for more efficient implementation and management of microservices architectures.

features.name: Product catalog and category management
features.description: Warehouse/catalog staff can create, update, deactivate and categorize products; retail customers can browse and search the catalog by category with product detail views.
features.scenario: A staff member adds a new product 'Espresso Machine X1' to the category 'Kitchen > Coffee', publishes it, and a retail customer immediately finds it when browsing the 'Coffee' category and opens its detail page.
acceptance_criteria: A product can be created with name, description, images, attributes and at least one category assignment
Categories can be created, renamed, nested and deactivated without deleting their products
Published products appear in category browsing and search results within one page refresh
Deactivated or unpublished products are not returned to customer-facing browsing
Catalog browse and product detail pages respond within the agreed responsiveness target under normal load

features.name: Product pricing
features.description: Each product carries a current sales price, with controlled price changes and price history so that prices shown to customers are consistent with prices used at checkout.
features.scenario: A pricing manager changes the price of 'Espresso Machine X1' from 499.00 to 449.00; the new price is shown on the product page, and a cart created after the change is priced at 449.00.
acceptance_criteria: Every sellable product has exactly one currently effective price per currency
Price changes are recorded with effective timestamp and the previous value is retained
Displayed price on the product page equals the price applied to newly added cart items
A price change never retroactively alters an already placed order

features.name: Shopping cart
features.description: Customers can add, update quantity of and remove catalog products in a persistent cart that shows the running total, and cart contents survive across sessions for identified customers.
features.scenario: A customer adds 2 units of 'Espresso Machine X1' to the cart, changes the quantity to 1, removes an unrelated item, logs out, logs back in and finds the cart with 1 unit and the correct total.
acceptance_criteria: Adding, updating quantity and removing items updates the cart total immediately
Cart contents persist for an identified customer across sessions
Only currently published and priced products can be added to the cart
Cart operations complete within the agreed responsiveness target under peak load

features.name: Order placement and management
features.description: Customers can convert a cart into an order via checkout; the order captures priced line items, is assigned a unique identifier and progresses through a defined lifecycle that customers and staff can view.
features.scenario: A customer with a valid cart submits checkout; an order in state 'Placed' with a unique order number is created, the cart is emptied, and the customer sees the order in the order history with its current status.
acceptance_criteria: Checkout produces an order with a unique identifier, snapshot of line items, quantities and prices
The cart is cleared only after the order has been successfully persisted
Order states (e.g. Placed, Paid, Fulfilled, Shipped, Cancelled, Rejected) transition only along defined allowed paths
Customers can list and view their own orders and current status; staff can view and search all orders
Submitting checkout twice for the same cart does not create duplicate orders

features.name: Payment processing
features.description: Placed orders are paid through a payment step that records payment attempts and results, and drives order state on success, failure or refund.
features.scenario: A customer pays for order #10245 by card; the payment is authorized and captured, the payment record is stored with the external reference, and the order moves to 'Paid'.
acceptance_criteria: A payment attempt is recorded for every checkout with amount, currency, method, timestamp and outcome
A successful payment transitions the order to 'Paid' exactly once, even if the confirmation is received more than once
A failed or declined payment leaves the order unpaid and allows the customer to retry
Refunds for cancelled orders are recorded and linked to the original payment
Payment outcome is never lost when a downstream step fails; unresolved payments are visible for reconciliation

features.name: Inventory and stock management
features.description: Stock levels per product are maintained by warehouse staff and by order events; stock is reserved at order placement and released on cancellation to prevent overselling.
features.scenario: Product 'Espresso Machine X1' has 3 units in stock; two customers concurrently order 2 units each â€” one order reserves 2 units and succeeds, the other is rejected or flagged as out of stock, and available stock reads 1.
acceptance_criteria: Warehouse staff can record stock receipts, corrections and write-offs per product
Order placement reserves stock and available stock is reduced accordingly
Concurrent orders exceeding available stock never result in a negative stock level
Cancelled or rejected orders release their reservation back to available stock
Customer-facing product pages reflect out-of-stock status

features.name: Shipping and delivery
features.description: Paid orders are handed to fulfilment: warehouse staff pick and dispatch shipments, tracking information is recorded, and customers can follow delivery status.
features.scenario: Order #10245 becomes 'Paid'; a shipment is created for the warehouse, staff mark it dispatched with tracking number TRK-77123, and the customer sees status 'Shipped' with the tracking number in the order details.
acceptance_criteria: A shipment is created for each order eligible for fulfilment with delivery address and line items
Warehouse staff can view the queue of shipments to be prepared and mark them dispatched/delivered
Tracking information is stored and visible to the customer on the order
Shipment status changes update the corresponding order status
No shipment is dispatched for an unpaid or cancelled order

features.name: Elastic handling of uneven traffic
features.description: Customer-facing browsing and purchasing capacity can be scaled independently of back-office fulfilment workloads so that traffic spikes are absorbed without degrading the whole application.
features.scenario: During a promotion, catalog browsing traffic rises to 10x the normal level while warehouse activity stays flat; browsing and checkout continue to meet response targets and warehouse operations are unaffected.
acceptance_criteria: Read-heavy customer-facing traffic can be scaled out without scaling back-office processing
A defined peak-load test (documented multiple of baseline traffic) passes with response times within target and no errors above the agreed threshold
Scaling changes require no code modification, only configuration/deployment changes
Back-office batch or warehouse workloads do not degrade customer-facing response times beyond the target

features.name: Reliable purchasing flow under partial failure
features.description: The core purchase chain (cart â†’ order â†’ payment â†’ stock reservation â†’ shipment) remains consistent when an individual step or dependency temporarily fails, with retries, idempotency and visible failure states.
features.scenario: The payment provider times out after authorizing payment for order #10250; on retry the system recognizes the existing authorization, does not charge twice, and the order reaches 'Paid' exactly once.
acceptance_criteria: Every state-changing purchase operation is idempotent with respect to retries and duplicate messages
A failure in a downstream step (payment, stock, shipping) never leaves an order in an undefined state
Failed operations are retried automatically and, after exhausting retries, are placed in a visible failure/dead-letter view for staff
A documented failure-injection test for each core step ends with consistent order, payment, stock and shipment data

features.name: Incremental modernization without business disruption
features.description: Modules of the existing Java modular monolith can be evolved or extracted one at a time, reusing the existing deployment and SQL technology, with the ability to release and roll back a single module without a big-bang migration.
features.scenario: The Sales module's checkout capability is changed and deployed while Portal, Warehouse, Billing and Shipping remain untouched; if a defect appears, the change is rolled back without affecting the other modules or requiring a full data migration.
acceptance_criteria: Each of Portal, Sales, Warehouse, Billing and Shipping has explicit module boundaries and documented interfaces
A change confined to one module can be built, tested, deployed and rolled back independently of the others
Existing SQL database and deployment approach are reused unless a documented justification for new infrastructure exists
No planned modernization step requires a full simultaneous cut-over of all modules
Automated regression tests for all core purchasing flows pass after each modernization step

features.name: Operational monitoring of core flows
features.description: Key business and technical indicators of the purchasing flow (traffic, response times, error rates, stuck orders and payments) are observable so that traffic spikes and failures are detected early.
features.scenario: During a traffic spike, checkout error rate rises above 2% for five minutes and an alert is raised, with a dashboard showing which step (payment, stock, shipping) is failing.
acceptance_criteria: Response time and error rate are measured for catalog browsing, cart, checkout and payment
Counts of stuck or failed orders, payments and shipments are visible to operators
Alerts fire when defined thresholds for response time or error rate are breached
A single request can be traced across the modules involved in the purchase flow

blueprint.rationale: The repository is already a well-bounded DDD modular monolith (Portal, Sales, Warehouse, Billing, Shipping) with in-process domain events and a single SQL schema, and the ArchUnit module tests (CleanModulesArchTest.java, CleanCodeArchTest.java) show the module seams are actively enforced. The stated drivers are the non-functional requirements 'Support higher and uneven traffic', 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' and 'Reliable core purchasing flows', plus maintainability, under an explicit cost-conscious, incremental, no-mandatory-cloud constraint. A full microservices decomposition would multiply operational cost without evidence of per-module scaling, ownership or compliance drivers. The smallest decomposition that satisfies the requirements is therefore: keep the monolith as the transactional core, extract only the read-heavy Catalog & Pricing capability (whose load profile is driven by browsing traffic and is independent of back-office fulfilment work), put an edge routing gateway in front for coexistence and independent scaling, and make cross-boundary domain events durable so the purchase flow stays consistent under partial failure. The pattern label names the transition because the target state is deliberately a monolith plus a small number of extracted services, reached incrementally.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Retail customers browse the catalog, build a cart, place an order, pay, and follow delivery status. Warehouse staff maintain stock, prepare and dispatch shipments, and review stuck orders or payments. Business stability is the primary constraint: nothing in this design requires a big-bang cut-over, and every step is releasable and reversible on its own. The change customers feel is that promotion-driven browsing spikes no longer degrade checkout, because catalog browsing runs on its own independently scalable service and back-office fulfilment work no longer competes with customer-facing requests â€” this is how the design meets 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions'. The change the business feels addresses 'Reliable core purchasing flows': the purchase chain (cart to order to payment to stock to shipment) survives a failing step because work is retried, duplicates are ignored, and anything that cannot complete becomes visible to staff instead of silently disappearing. The change the delivery team feels is that catalog/pricing can be changed and deployed on its own cadence, while Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module keep the low-friction single-deployment model they have today. Costs stay bounded: the existing Java/Spring stack and existing relational database technology are retained, and the only genuinely new infrastructure is a message broker, an edge gateway and an observability stack, each justified by a stated requirement.
blueprint.technical_view:
Target state. Two deployables plus supporting infrastructure. (1) Commerce Core Application â€” the existing Spring Boot Java monolith, retaining the Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module, Shipping Delivery Module and Storefront Portal, backed by the Core Commerce SQL Database. (2) Catalog & Pricing Service â€” a separately deployable Spring Boot Java service owning product, category and price data in the Catalog & Pricing Database. In front of both sits the Edge Routing Gateway, which routes customer-facing catalog and product-detail traffic to the Catalog & Pricing Service and everything else to the Storefront Portal, allowing the two deployables to be scaled with different replica counts and enabling gradual traffic shifting during extraction. This routing seam is the direct technical answer to the non-functional requirements 'Support higher and uneven traffic' and 'Responsive customer-facing interactions'.

Communication. Within the Commerce Core Application, modules keep their current in-process, interface-based collaboration and their existing DDD domain events (OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, DeliveryPrepared, DeliveryDispatched, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed) â€” this preserves the transactional consistency of the purchase chain in one database and avoids distributed transactions where no driver demands them. Cross-boundary communication (Commerce Core Application to/from Catalog & Pricing Service) is asynchronous over the Domain Event Backbone for state propagation (price and publication changes, out-of-stock signals) and synchronous HTTP only where a request must be answered inline (price/availability validation when an item is added to the cart, priced-line-item snapshot at checkout). Every event published across a boundary is written through a transactional outbox in the publisher's own database and relayed to the broker, so publication is atomic with the state change that caused it.

Reliability â€” this is the design's explicit answer to the non-functional requirement 'Reliable core purchasing flows'. Each state-changing purchase operation carries an idempotency key (cart-id/checkout-token for order placement, payment reference for payment confirmation, order-id for dispatch), so retries and duplicate deliveries converge to one effect. The existing DispatchingSaga is generalised into the choreographed compensation model for the order lifecycle: stock reservation failure rejects the order and releases the reservation, payment failure leaves the order unpaid and retryable, and exhausted retries land in a dead-letter view surfaced to staff. Failure-injection tests per core step validate that order, payment, stock and shipment data stay consistent.

Data. No store migration. The Core Commerce SQL Database remains the existing relational schema; catalog, category and price tables move to the Catalog & Pricing Database as part of extraction, with the Commerce Core Application keeping only the product identifiers and priced snapshots it already persists in orders and cart items. Cross-boundary reads are by identifier plus cached projection, never by shared table access; schema-level separation is introduced before the physical split so the split is a deployment event rather than a rewrite.

Observability. The Observability & Alerting Stack collects metrics, logs and distributed traces from the Edge Routing Gateway, the Storefront Portal, the Catalog & Pricing Service, all domain modules and the Domain Event Backbone, exposes response time and error rate per flow (browse, cart, checkout, payment) and counts of stuck orders, payments and shipments, and raises alerts on agreed thresholds. Thresholds and peak-load multiples are to be agreed and measured; no numeric target is asserted here.

constraints_addressed: Cloud: no provider mandated; all components are deployable on the existing runtime (JVM/Spring Boot, container or VM) and are provider-neutral. Managed equivalents may be substituted without design change.

Budget: exactly one service is extracted; the remaining four domain modules stay in the existing deployable. New infrastructure is limited to a message broker, a gateway and an observability stack, each tied to a stated requirement.

Non-functional 'Support higher and uneven traffic': read-heavy catalog/pricing traffic is separated behind the Edge Routing Gateway and scales independently of back-office fulfilment (FEAT-008). No numeric peak target is asserted; the peak-load multiple must be agreed and measured.

Non-functional 'Responsive customer-facing interactions': browse and product-detail load is removed from the transactional deployable, per-flow response time is measured by the Observability & Alerting Stack, and the responsiveness target is to be agreed with the business rather than asserted here.

Non-functional 'Reliable core purchasing flows': the purchase chain keeps single-database transactional consistency in the Core Commerce SQL Database, cross-boundary events are published through a transactional outbox, all state-changing operations are idempotent, compensation is choreographed via the dispatching saga, and exhausted retries surface in a dead-letter view (FEAT-009).
Compliance: no compliance requirements were stated. Payment card data is not stored; only provider references are persisted, keeping cardholder-data scope out of the system.
Migration: strangler-fig sequence with schema separation before physical split, dual-routing during extraction, and no step requiring simultaneous cut-over of all modules (FEAT-010).
assumptions: Assumption: the application is Spring Boot based (Maven wrapper, Thymeleaf templates, JDBC repositories in the repository), and Spring's in-process ApplicationEventPublisher backs the current EventPublisher abstraction.

Assumption: peak traffic is dominated by anonymous catalog browsing and product-detail reads rather than by checkout write volume; this is the premise for extracting Catalog & Pricing first and must be confirmed with production traffic data.

Assumption: the current deployment is a single instance or a small horizontally scaled set of the monolith behind an existing entry point; the Edge Routing Gateway replaces or fronts that entry point.

Assumption: customer identity/session handling exists sufficiently for cart persistence across sessions (repository shows cart identification via cookies); identified-customer cart persistence (FEAT-003) may require an identity capability not present in the repository.
Assumption: the exact responsiveness, availability and error-rate targets are not yet defined; acceptance criteria are stated qualitatively until the business agrees numbers.
open_risks: Risk: extracting Catalog & Pricing introduces a synchronous dependency from Sales Cart Module at add-to-cart time; if the Catalog & Pricing Service is unavailable, add-to-cart fails. Mitigation (to be designed): short-lived price/publication cache in the Commerce Core Application with an explicit staleness bound.

Risk: price consistency between display and checkout across a service boundary (FEAT-002) depends on the priced snapshot being taken at cart-add and re-validated at checkout; a race remains between price change and checkout and must be resolved by an agreed business rule.
Risk: the repository shows no existing message broker; introducing the Domain Event Backbone adds an operational component the team may not yet run, plus outbox relay and dead-letter handling.
Risk: FEAT-003's cross-session cart persistence for identified customers has no visible identity/authentication capability in the repository; scope may be larger than this design assumes.

Risk: FEAT-001 catalog authoring (create/update/deactivate/publish) is only partially evidenced in the repository (read-side finders dominate); the write side of catalog management may need to be built rather than extracted.

Risk: without agreed numeric SLOs, the peak-load and failure-injection acceptance criteria in FEAT-008 and FEAT-009 cannot yet be validated objectively, so the 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirement can currently only be validated qualitatively.

migration_steps.title: Harden module seams and establish baseline observability
migration_steps.objective: Make the current modular monolith measurable and its boundaries explicit before anything moves, so later steps are low-risk and their effect is visible. First because every subsequent step depends on knowing the real traffic profile and on enforced boundaries.
changes: Extend the existing ArchUnit module tests so every cross-module call goes through a published module interface only.

Deploy the Observability & Alerting Stack and instrument Storefront Portal, Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module with metrics, logs and distributed tracing.
Measure the real traffic split between catalog browsing and transactional flows to confirm the extraction premise.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: No structural or data change; the Commerce Core Application remains the single deployable against the Core Commerce SQL Database.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Per-flow response time and error rate are visible for browse, cart, checkout and payment, and boundary tests fail on any direct cross-module internal access.

migration_steps.title: Separate catalog and pricing schema ownership inside the Core Commerce SQL Database
migration_steps.objective: Turn the future service boundary into a data boundary while still inside one deployable, so the later physical split is a deployment event rather than a rewrite. Second because data coupling, not code coupling, is the expensive part of extraction.
changes: Move product, category and price tables into a dedicated schema within the Core Commerce SQL Database owned solely by the catalog and pricing code.
Replace any join-based cross-module access to those tables from Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module and Warehouse Inventory Module with calls to the catalog module interface.
Confirm that Sales Order Module persists a priced line-item snapshot so orders never depend on live price lookups.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Single database instance, two logically owned schemas; all access remains transactional and in-process, so no consistency change occurs yet.
migration_steps.exit_condition: No SQL statement outside the catalog and pricing code references catalog, category or price tables.

migration_steps.title: Introduce the Domain Event Backbone with a transactional outbox
migration_steps.objective: Provide durable, retryable, idempotent cross-boundary messaging before any boundary becomes a network boundary, directly serving the 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirement. Third because the extracted service and the reliability requirement (FEAT-009) both depend on it.
changes: Deploy the Domain Event Backbone (message broker) and add an outbox table plus relay to the Core Commerce SQL Database.

Route the existing OrderPlaced, PaymentCollected, GoodsFetched, GoodsMissed, DeliveryPrepared and DeliveryDispatched domain events through the outbox, keeping delivery semantics compatible with today's listeners.
Add idempotency keys and consumer-side deduplication to Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module and Shipping Delivery Module, and add a dead-letter view for staff.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Events are published atomically with their state change via the outbox; in-process listeners are migrated one event type at a time, with the previous in-process path removable per event type after verification.
migration_steps.exit_condition: A documented failure-injection test on payment, stock and shipping steps leaves order, payment, stock and shipment data consistent, and exhausted retries appear in the dead-letter view.

migration_steps.title: Introduce the Edge Routing Gateway in front of the Commerce Core Application
migration_steps.objective: Create the routing seam that later allows traffic to be shifted to an extracted service and allows differential scaling, with no behavioural change. Fourth because it must be proven neutral before it carries a split.
changes: Deploy the Edge Routing Gateway as the single entry point for retail customers and warehouse staff.
Route all traffic to the Storefront Portal of the Commerce Core Application initially.
Emit gateway request metrics and traces to the Observability & Alerting Stack.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Pass-through routing only; the Commerce Core Application is unchanged and the gateway can be bypassed to roll back.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All customer and staff traffic flows through the Edge Routing Gateway with unchanged functional behaviour and no measurable regression against the step-1 baseline.

migration_steps.title: Extract the Catalog & Pricing Service and its Catalog & Pricing Database
migration_steps.objective: Deliver the actual scaling benefit by making the read-heavy browsing capability independently deployable and scalable. Fifth because it is only safe once seams, data ownership, messaging and routing exist.
changes: Deploy the Catalog & Pricing Service as a separate Spring Boot Java deployable built from the extracted catalog and pricing code.
Promote the separated catalog schema into the standalone Catalog & Pricing Database.
Point Sales Cart Module at the Catalog & Pricing Service over HTTP for price and publication validation, with caching and a defined degraded behaviour.
Subscribe the Catalog & Pricing Service to out-of-stock events from Warehouse Inventory Module via the Domain Event Backbone.
Shift catalog browse and product-detail routes on the Edge Routing Gateway from the Storefront Portal to the Catalog & Pricing Service progressively.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Progressive traffic shifting at the Edge Routing Gateway with the monolith's catalog read path retained as fallback until the shift is complete; catalog data is migrated once and the monolith's catalog tables are dropped only after the fallback is retired.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All catalog browse and product-detail traffic is served by the Catalog & Pricing Service, the Commerce Core Application no longer reads catalog tables, and full regression tests for all core purchasing flows pass.

migration_steps.title: Tune independent scaling and validate the target state
migration_steps.objective: Confirm the modernization actually satisfies the 'Support higher and uneven traffic', 'Responsive customer-facing interactions' and 'Reliable core purchasing flows' requirements, and formally record what remains in the monolith. Last because it validates the whole sequence.
changes: Configure independent replica counts and autoscaling policies for the Catalog & Pricing Service and the Commerce Core Application via deployment configuration only.
Run an agreed peak-load test against browsing and checkout with warehouse workload held flat, and a failure-injection test per core step.

Record the explicit decision that Sales Cart Module, Sales Order Module, Billing Payment Module, Warehouse Inventory Module, Shipping Delivery Module and Storefront Portal are retained in the Commerce Core Application, with further extraction deferred until a concrete scaling, ownership or availability driver appears.
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Steady target state: two deployables, two databases, one event backbone; further extraction is explicitly deferred, not implied.
migration_steps.exit_condition: The agreed peak-load and failure-injection tests pass within the thresholds the business has by then defined, and alerts fire correctly when those thresholds are breached.
